To interweave means to weave two or more things together so that they cross through and over each other, becoming tightly connected — almost inseparable — as a single, unified whole.

The key image to hold in your mind is a piece of woven fabric. In fabric, horizontal threads cross over and under vertical threads, back and forth, again and again. No single thread just sits next to another — each thread passes through the others. That crossing, locking pattern is what "interweave" captures. The individual threads are still there, but together they form something much larger and stronger.

In its most direct, physical sense, to interweave means to literally weave things together — threads, strips, branches, ribbons, reeds, or any flexible material.

For example:

  • A basket-maker interweaves thin strips of wood to create a basket.
  • A craft artist interweaves ribbons of different colors to make a decorative braid.
  • Vines in a forest can interweave as they grow, forming a thick, tangled canopy.

In each case, the materials don't just touch — they pass through each other in an alternating, crossing pattern.

This is where the word truly comes alive, and where you'll encounter it most often.

When used figuratively, interweave means to combine abstract things — ideas, stories, emotions, themes, events, cultures — so closely and deeply that they become part of one another. They don't just exist alongside each other; they cross through each other, the way threads do in cloth.

Here are some clear examples:

  • A novelist might interweave two separate storylines throughout a book — jumping from one story to the other and back, so that the two plots feel connected and support each other, rather than being completely separate.
  • A great speech might interweave humor and sadness — the two emotions don't come in separate, isolated blocks; they blend through each other so that you're laughing and feeling moved at the same time.
  • Music composers often interweave multiple melodies — each melody weaves through the others, so you can hear them individually but they also sound like one unified piece.
  • Historians say that the histories of two neighboring countries are deeply interwoven — meaning the events of one country are so tangled up with those of the other that you cannot fully understand one without the other.

What makes "interweave" different from simpler words like mix or combine is the sense of deep, structural connection.

When things are interwoven:

1. They cross through each other, not just sit next to each other.
Two colors of paint that are mixed blend and disappear into each other. But two colors of thread that are interwoven stay distinct — you can still see each color — yet they are locked together in a crossing structure. Interweave preserves the identity of the individual parts while joining them tightly.

2. They support and depend on each other.
In woven fabric, each thread holds the others in place. Pull one thread out and the fabric weakens or falls apart. When ideas, stories, or themes are interwoven, they similarly hold each other up. Remove one, and the whole feels incomplete.

3. Separating them is hard.
Things that have been interwoven are not easy to pull apart. This is a strong, structural kind of blending — not a loose or casual mixing.

Since you want a complete picture, here are the different forms of the verb:

  • To interweave — the base/infinitive form. ("They decided to interweave the two melodies.")
  • Interweaves — third person singular, present tense. ("She interweaves personal stories into her lectures.")
  • Interweaving — present participle, used for ongoing action. ("He is interweaving several themes in his novel.")
  • Interwove — simple past tense. ("The director interwove the two storylines beautifully.")
  • Interwoven — past participle, used with "have/has/had" or as an adjective. ("The themes are interwoven throughout the poem." / "The two cultures have long been interwoven.")

Note that interwoven is especially useful and common as an adjective — you'll often see it used to describe something that has already been woven together: "Their lives were deeply interwoven."

Knowing related words will sharpen your understanding of exactly what "interweave" means.

Intertwine — very close in meaning. Intertwine suggests things twisting around each other (think of two vines spiraling around each other). Interweave specifically evokes the over-and-under, crossing pattern of weaving. In practice, people use these almost interchangeably.

Interlace — nearly identical to interweave. It emphasizes a lacing or crossing pattern, like shoelaces. Very similar feel.

Blend — to mix things together smoothly until distinctions are reduced. Blend feels more like stirring; interweave feels more like structured crossing.

Merge — to combine things so that they lose their separate identities and become one thing. When things merge, the individual parts disappear. When things interweave, the individual parts are still somewhat identifiable — the threads are still visible in the cloth.

Knit — to join or connect closely. Used figuratively ("a tightly knit community"), but without the visual sense of crossing threads that interweave carries.

These are words that mean the opposite:

  • Separate — to pull apart or keep apart.
  • Disentangle — to undo something that has become tangled or interwoven.
  • Unravel — to undo a woven or tangled structure, thread by thread.
  • Isolate — to keep something alone, away from everything else.

Think of "interweave" as a word that always carries the image of a loom — of threads crossing over and under each other in a deliberate, structured pattern, creating something unified and strong. Whether you're talking about actual threads, or stories, or ideas, or cultures, or emotions — to interweave them is to bring them together in a crossing, locking, mutually-supporting way, so that the result is more than the sum of its parts, and pulling them apart would damage the whole.
